synthesis.headline: Central-Plains heat ridge holds and reloads while a genuine PV intrusion and cutoff over the Canadian Prairies drive the northern-stream storms — and a Gulf low spins up toward the Texas coast
synthesis.narrative:
North America stays under an amplified longwave pattern, but the organizing story today is a division of labor between a hot, subsident central-continent ridge and an unusually active northern tier. At 500 mb a broad late-summer ridge crests near 592-594 dam over the central Plains, faced west by a deep trough digging into the Pacific Northwest and western Canada. The distinctive feature is a closed low over south-central Canada just north of the northern Plains (roughly 563-566 dam), negatively tilted and apparently pivoting or retrogressing rather than translating cleanly downstream. At the surface the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. sits under a sprawling but modest high (centers near 1021-1022 mb — an ordinary summer anticyclonic belt, not strong suppression), with slack gradients away from the boundaries. The action is on the edges: a stationary front draped along the Gulf Coast from Texas to Florida with upper-70s dewpoints, and — across the border — a genuinely busy Canadian map, where a strong 1037 hPa Pacific high anchors the West while a cluster of 996-1003 hPa lows with cold and occluded fronts churns over Ontario, Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces, trailing fronts into the northeastern U.S. That northeastern-quadrant frontal complex holds the tightest gradient on the Canadian analysis.

Today's centers of action: first, the Gulf. GOES Air Mass RGB shows a compact, tightly curved cluster of deep convection with a clear cyclonic curl near the Texas-Louisiana coast — the low that NHC gives a 70 percent chance of becoming a short-lived depression or storm before it reaches the upper Texas/southwestern Louisiana coast Tuesday, with heavy rain regardless. Second, the Southwest: WPC carries a Moderate Risk of excessive rainfall over the Great Basin today from monsoonal moisture, with flash flooding and likely debris flows on burn scars — the highest-end flood threat on the board. Third, the northern-stream storms: SPC has a Marginal Risk today across the Great Lakes, central Plains, and Great Basin (a shortwave into Wisconsin/Upper Michigan with 2500+ J/kg MLCAPE along the cold front), and the threat shifts Tuesday to a Slight Risk over the Lower Great Lakes, Northeast, and northern Mid-Atlantic ahead of the advancing front. Meanwhile dangerous heat builds over the Middle Mississippi Valley and central/southern Plains.

The upper-level context ties it together. The broad orange-red over the central and southeastern U.S. on the Air Mass imagery is warm, dry, low-PV air under the ridge — subsidence, midlevel warming, and capping (not the modest surface highs) are what build and hold the heat and suppress convection there. Contrast that with the full-disk view over Canada, where a compact, strongly red feature over the Alberta-Saskatchewan Prairies, elongated on the cyclonic flank of the trough, reads as a real high-PV stratospheric intrusion — the dynamic engine behind the northern-tier cutoff and the sharp airmass boundary/implied jet corridor that arcs from the northern Rockies through the Great Lakes into New England. Impulses riding that boundary on the ridge's northern flank are what fire the Great Lakes and, tomorrow, Northeast storms. On the regime question, read the ensemble pair against WPC: the 6-10 day (Sep 5-9) keeps a large positive height anomaly over the Canadian Arctic with the ridge axis running meridionally through the western interior, but the zero line sits along the Rockies so the ridge is anchored north over Canada, not the western CONUS. By 8-14 day (Sep 7-13) that Arctic anchor reverses — it becomes a closed low with a modest negative departure — while the CONUS ridge survives in absolute heights (588 dam into the central/northern Rockies) but loses its anomaly signature, reading near climatology, with below-normal heights hanging on over the southern Plains and Gulf at both leads. WPC's days 3-7, however, explicitly keeps the ridge retrograding and reamplifying back over the central U.S. after a brief weekend front, holding the core heat over the Plains and Mid/Lower Mississippi Valley into next week. The synthesis: near term the central heat is not going anywhere and even reloads in place — the weekend front is temporary flattening, not a regime change — but its anomalous character fades with time, and the genuinely transitioning piece is the high-latitude block, which yesterday looked like the durable element and now collapses by the 8-14 lead. That is a real break from the last few days' read.
synthesis.climate_context: This is peak-season North America running close to the seasonal script, with the Atlantic basin at its early-September climatological maximum, an active North American Monsoon feeding daily high-terrain and Great Basin convection, and severe weather expressing itself as ridge-periphery, northern-stream and frontal storms rather than deep-Plains outbreaks. The ENSO backdrop is a developing warm state: the ONI has climbed from weak La Niña in late 2025 to roughly +1.39C by May-July 2026, a transition toward El Niño. That configuration typically favors an active eastern Pacific while shear and dry air lean against the Atlantic, and the current tropics fit the split — a 90 percent development area south-southwest of Mexico and a separate area near Hawaii against a comparatively quieter Atlantic, where Dolly's remnants and the homegrown Gulf low carry the only near-term odds (the Gulf remaining capable of spinning up its own systems regardless of basin-wide shear). Teleconnection indices lag the height field and are used only as a cross-check: the decisively negative NAO (-0.90) and negative PNA (-0.70) are directionally supportive of high-latitude blocking and eastern troughing, but note the mismatch with the 8-14 day guidance that collapses the Arctic block — a reminder that these are weak summer signals that should not override the height and PV fields.
synthesis.regional_notes: SPC has no active mesoscale discussions and no organized convective threat under monitoring as of this briefing. The standout sub-synoptic threat is the Great Basin Moderate Risk of excessive rainfall — numerous flash floods possible with debris flows likely over recently burned terrain, slot canyons, and urban areas. Along the Gulf, daily heavy rain persists on the moist side of the stationary front across the Deep South and Florida, with the developing Texas/Louisiana coastal low adding locally heavy rainfall Tuesday-Wednesday. In Canada, the notable gradient runs through the northeastern frontal complex over Ontario, Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces. In the tropics beyond the Gulf, Dolly's remnants continue to bring locally heavy rain and gusty winds across the Leewards, Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico, Hispaniola, and the Bahamas (only 10 percent redevelopment), and full-disk imagery shows a spiraling cloud mass east of the Lesser Antilles and vigorous convection near the Yucatan worth watching.

sources.title: Surface Analysis
sources.summary:
The chart is valid 0900Z Monday 31 August 2026. The most prominent features are a sprawling high-pressure complex across the central and eastern U.S., with centers reading near 1022 mb over the upper Midwest, 1022 mb along the mid-Atlantic coast, and 1021 mb over the Carolinas area — all modest late-summer values that simply reflect the broad anticyclonic belt rather than any anomalously strong suppression. A low near 1006 mb sits over the southern Plains or Oklahoma region, with another low of similar depth over the Desert Southwest near 1006-1008 mb; these are likely thermally driven given the season. A cold front extends from the upper-Midwest low southwestward, and a warm front or stationary boundary appears draped across the northern tier from the Great Lakes westward, where the tightest isobar spacing on the chart concentrates — that region from the northern Plains into the upper Great Lakes shows the most compressed gradient and therefore the greatest implied wind forcing at the surface.

A separate frontal boundary, appearing stationary or slow-moving, lies across the Gulf Coast states from roughly Texas into Florida, where dew points in the upper 70s°F are plotted, indicating deep low-level moisture convergence along that boundary; that zone, combined with the nearby low pressure, is where this chart most clearly focuses surface lift and moisture. The remainder of the eastern two-thirds of the country under the high centers shows slack, open isobar spacing, meaning surface forcing there is minimal and any convection would depend on upper-level or mesoscale mechanisms the chart cannot show. The Pacific Northwest shows a weak low near 1009 mb with an associated front along the coast, but isobars are relatively open inland.

sources.title: Canadian Surface Analysis
sources.summary: This CMC 0000Z surface analysis valid 31 August 2026 shows a broad high pressure ridge of 1037 hPa centered well out over the central North Pacific, with its eastern flank extending a weakening anticyclonic influence toward the British Columbia coast. Across the western Canadian interior, pressure values in the low 1020s suggest generally tranquil conditions, though a cluster of lows and frontal boundaries is packed into the central and eastern portions of the domain at latitudes that, judged against the visible coastlines of Hudson Bay and the Great Lakes, place active frontal activity roughly over Ontario, Quebec, and the Atlantic provinces, where several centers between 996 and 1003 hPa are analyzed with cold and occluded fronts trailing southward into the northeastern United States. The tightest gradients on the chart appear across that northeastern quadrant, where the spacing of isobars between the 996-997 hPa lows and a 1022 hPa high to their west implies a focused wind field, consistent with a broad area of lift and moisture convergence along those frontal zones straddling the Canada-US border from the Great Lakes eastward. Tropical Depression Bang-Lang is labeled at 36.7N 165.3E, placing it in the western North Pacific well outside the North American domain and carrying no direct influence on the Canadian pattern shown. In the upper portion of the frame, several lows in the 994-1002 hPa range are plotted over what the polar projection places in high Arctic waters or the Canadian Archipelago, where such values are unremarkable at this time of year and should not be read as significant mid-latitude systems.

sources.title: 500 mb Analysis
sources.summary:
The 500 mb pattern at 1200 UTC 31 August 2026 shows a high-amplitude longwave configuration with a pronounced ridge centered over the north-central United States, where heights reach approximately 592-594 dam over the central Plains, and a deep trough digging across the Pacific Northwest and western Canada. A closed low is evident over south-central Canada just north of the U.S. border near the northern Plains, with a clearly closed contour around roughly 563-566 dam, indicating it has separated from the main westerlies and is functioning as a cutoff rather than a translating open wave. This cutoff tilts slightly negatively (southwest-northeast) based on the contour orientation, consistent with a system that is retrogressing or pivoting rather than moving progressively downstream.

The green shading, which by this product's color scale marks the implied strongest wind corridor, sweeps in a broad arc from the Pacific across far southern Canada and then curves anticyclonically southward ahead of the cutoff, suggesting a jet streak oriented roughly west-northwest to east-northeast across the northern tier, with the exit region near the Great Lakes. A separate low-pressure center marked over the western Atlantic southeast of the Carolinas appears as an open or weakly closed system at this level. The overall pattern is not strongly progressive — the ridge-cutoff dipole over the central continent and the apparent retrograde tendency of the northern Plains cutoff suggest retarded downstream translation, though the chart alone does not confirm full blocking by classic geometric criteria.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 Air Mass RGB valid 31 August 2026 at 1321Z shows a broad orange-red signature dominating the central and southeastern United States, consistent with dry upper-tropospheric air under a summer ridge rather than a stratospheric intrusion. A compact, tightly curved cluster of bright white deep convection sits over the central Gulf Coast states, near the Texas-Louisiana border area, with a clear cyclonic curl visible in the surrounding cloud field, indicating an organized low-level circulation. A second area of curved cloud structure lies over the western Atlantic, roughly east of the Florida-Georgia coast, also showing signs of organization but with less concentrated cold tops. The sharpest airmass boundary — and implied jet corridor — runs across the northern tier from the northern Rockies through the Great Lakes and into New England, where the orange dry air to the south gives way abruptly to the more muted green-yellow tones associated with the baroclinic zone. Elongated mid-level cloud streaks along this boundary are consistent with anticyclonic outflow from the northern convection and suggest the boundary is active, though no wind data are plotted to confirm speeds.

sources.title: Air Mass RGB Full Disk (GOES-19)
sources.summary: This GOES-19 AirMass RGB from 31 August 2026 at 1320Z shows a sharp airmass boundary arcing across central Canada, where deep red-orange dry upper-tropospheric air on the poleward side gives way abruptly to the green moist tropical airmass across the central and southern United States. A compact, strongly red-colored feature is visible over the Canadian Prairies near the Alberta-Saskatchewan area, elongated on the cyclonic flank of a trough, which is consistent with a genuine high-PV stratospheric intrusion rather than simple ridge subsidence. Across the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico, several areas of bright white convective cloud tops are embedded within the broad green moist airmass, with the most vigorous cluster positioned over or just east of the Yucatan Peninsula, suggesting an area of organized deep convection possibly associated with a tropical wave; a second area of spiraling cloud sits over the open Atlantic well east of the Lesser Antilles and merits attention as a potential tropical development zone. The South American interior is largely clear and green-toned, indicating a warm moist airmass with little upper-level cloud, while the southern tip of the continent and the surrounding Southern Ocean show the characteristic blue-purple cold dry upper air and active frontal cloud bands.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day Temperature Outlook
sources.summary: The dominant feature is a broad above-normal signal covering essentially the entire contiguous US east of the Rockies, with the highest probabilities, 90-100 percent, centered on a compact bull's-eye straddling the Kansas-Oklahoma border and extending into northern Texas. Probabilities drop concentrically outward but remain in the 60-70 percent range across most of the Southeast, Great Lakes, and mid-Atlantic, indicating a widespread and confident warm signal rather than a marginal one. The only below-normal region in the lower 48 is the Pacific Northwest and interior Northwest, where probabilities reach 50-60 percent below normal centered roughly over Washington and Oregon, with a near-normal transition zone across Nevada and southern Idaho separating the two regimes. The sharp contrast between the cool Northwest and the intensely warm central Plains is consistent with a persistent amplified upper-level ridge anchored over the south-central Plains and a trough or lower heights maintained over the Northeast Pacific into the Northwest, implying that whatever pattern is driving the current warm episode over the central US is expected by the CPC to remain largely intact through September 5-9 rather than break down. Alaska shows a similar split, with below-normal probabilities over the interior and North Slope and above-normal probabilities along the southern coast and Alaska Peninsula, consistent with an offshore trough-ridge couplet; Hawaii carries a 60-70 percent above-normal signal statewide.

sources.title: CPC 6-10 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary:
This is indeed a CPC 6-10 day 500 mb height and height anomaly forecast, valid 5-9 September 2026, with heights in dam (green solid contours at 60 dam intervals) and anomalies in dam (dashed contours, red positive and blue negative).

The dominant feature is a strongly positive anomaly center over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago and northern Hudson Bay, where the anomaly contours reach approximately +90 dam — this reads as an extraordinarily large value and is almost certainly a misread of contours labeled in meters rather than dam; the true anomaly is more likely in the range of +9 dam or the labeling unit differs from what the legend states, so treat the relative magnitude as large positive rather than the face value. The ridge axis in absolute heights runs roughly meridionally from the central Canadian Arctic southward through the western interior of North America, with 588 dam contours arching across the central Rockies into the central United States. A trough axis is implied by the height gradient and negative anomaly zone (blue dashed, around -30 units) extending across the northeastern Pacific and into the Pacific Northwest and British Columbia coast, with another area of negative anomalies visible over the southeastern United States near the Gulf Coast.

The zero anomaly line cuts across the western contiguous United States roughly along the Rockies corridor, meaning positive anomalies do not extend deeply into the western lower 48 — the ridge is centered well to the north over Canada rather than being anchored over the western CONUS. The pattern shows a highly amplified, positively tilted ridge over Arctic Canada rather than a classic western ridge, and the relatively zonal spacing of height contours across the central and eastern United States suggests near-normal or slightly below-normal flow there, with amplification concentrated at high latitudes rather than mid-latitudes.

sources.title: CPC 8-14 Day 500 mb Height Outlook
sources.summary: This chart is a 500 mb height and height-anomaly (departure from normal) prognostic valid 7–13 September 2026, made 30 August 2026, with heights contoured in solid green at 60 m intervals and anomalies in dashed red (negative) and dashed blue (positive). The dominant feature is a deep closed low centered over the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, with the innermost contour near 510 dam; the height anomaly dashes in that region appear to show a modest negative departure, though the anomaly contours there are somewhat crowded and difficult to read precisely. Over the western contiguous United States and extending into the northern Rockies and northern Plains, the height field shows a strong ridge with the 588 dam contour reaching into the central and northern Rockies and the 576–582 dam surface broadly covering the western two-thirds of the lower 48; the positive anomaly dashed blue contours appear largely absent from this western ridge region, suggesting the ridge amplitude is near or only slightly above climatology rather than strongly anomalous. Critically, there is no clearly defined positive anomaly center over western Canada or the northern Plains — the blue dashed anomaly contours visible in the upper-right portion of the chart are positioned over far northeastern Canada and Greenland, not over the northern Rockies corridor — so the ridge appears to be centered in the interior West but without a strong positive departure anchoring it northward into western Canada. The southern United States shows the 588 dam contour sagging into the south-central Plains, and negative anomaly contours (red dashed, labeled around -30 in apparent units) appear in the southern Plains and Gulf Coast region, consistent with a trough or below-normal heights at those latitudes.

sources.title: WPC Short Range Forecast Discussion
sources.summary: Moderate Risk of excessive rainfall over the Great Basin Monday from monsoonal moisture; numerous flash flooding events possible with debris flows likely in recently burned areas. Slight Risk of excessive rainfall over Western/Central Gulf Coast Tuesday-Wednesday from weak low pressure. Slight Risk of severe thunderstorms Tuesday over Lower Great Lakes, Northeast, and Northern Mid-Atlantic ahead of a frontal boundary moving from the Plains to Great Lakes by Wednesday; hazards include frequent lightning, severe winds, hail, and tornadoes. Additional scattered thunderstorms expected across Southwest, Central/Southern Rockies, and Central Plains Monday. Weakening front approaches Northwest Coast early Tuesday, rain spreading inland by afternoon. Heat building over Middle Mississippi Valley and Central/Southern Plains Monday-Tuesday.

sources.title: SPC Day 1 Convective Outlook
sources.summary: Marginal risk of severe thunderstorms this afternoon and evening across the Great Lakes region, central Plains, and Great Basin. Upper Midwest: Shortwave trough moving northeast into Wisconsin and upper Michigan by late afternoon with strong heating, upper 60s to lower 70s dewpoints, and MLCAPE over 2500 J/kg. Cold front focus supporting scattered thunderstorms; sufficient vertical shear may enable rotating storms with damaging winds and hail. Eastern Colorado into Nebraska: Mid-level moisture plume continues; afternoon mountain storms spreading eastward into eastern Colorado with strong outflow winds possible; isolated strong storms may persist into northwest Kansas and Nebraska after dark. Utah/Arizona: Shortwave trough moving east from California providing large-scale forcing; scattered afternoon thunderstorms with locally damaging wind gusts possible if sufficient heating develops.

sources.title: SPC Mesoscale Discussions
sources.summary: No active mesoscale discussions from SPC. No organized convective threat is currently under active monitoring.

sources.title: NHC Tropical Weather Outlooks
sources.summary:
Atlantic: Low pressure south of Louisiana with concentrated convection is likely to become a short-lived tropical depression or tropical storm before reaching the Upper Texas or southwestern Louisiana coast Tuesday, with 70 percent formation probability. Locally heavy rainfall expected regardless. Remnants of Tropical Storm Dolly near Hispaniola remain disorganized, moving west-northwest at 20-25 mph into unfavorable upper-level winds with only 10 percent seven-day redevelopment chance, though locally heavy rains and gusty winds possible across the Leewards, Virgin Islands, Puerto Rico, Hispaniola, and Bahamas.

East Pacific: Broad low pressure south-southwest of southwestern Mexico showing organization with favorable conditions; tropical depression or tropical storm expected to form later today or tonight while moving northwest at 10 mph, with 90 percent formation probability. Separate area of low pressure could develop south or southwest of Hawaii in a couple days with 20 percent seven-day development chance.

sources.title: ENSO State (Oceanic Niño Index)
sources.summary: The Oceanic Niño Index shows sea surface temperatures currently running slightly below normal through early 2026, consistent with weak La Niña conditions. Anomalies are modest negative through March 2026, then trend sharply warmer through summer 2026. By May-July 2026, anomalies reach +1.39°C above normal, indicating a transition toward El Niño conditions. The shift from cool to warm is notable and sustained over the forecast period.

sources.title: Teleconnection Indices (PNA, AO, NAO)
sources.summary: PNA has weakened and turned moderately negative, with the 7-day mean falling to -0.70, supporting eastern North American trough development rather than western ridge. AO bounced sharply positive mid-period (reaching +1.67) before dropping back to -0.35, suggesting recent weakening of high-latitude blocking support. NAO has swung decisively negative (7-day mean -0.90, down from +0.19), now favoring blocking patterns that could trap eastern systems. Note these are summer indices with inherently weak signals; the NAO's sharp recent drop is the most notable feature, potentially supporting Atlantic cutoff scenarios.
